snippet.title: Староверы - отшельники: Жизнь старообрядцев в Енисейской Тайге / Как живут люди / Россия, Тыва
snippet.description:
Люди, сегодня я покажу вам, как Люди живут в пожалуй самых загадочных и закрытых деревнях. Здесь не то что снимать трудно: большинство староверов к себе даже гостей чужих не пускает. По их внутренним правилам в их деревнях запрещено пользоваться сотовыми телефонами, смотреть телевизор, слушать радио… они почти никогда не пьют из одной бутылки с другими людьми, и еще реже садятся есть за стол с гостями. Но несмотря на все эти запреты, мы все же доплывем до самой закрытой и самой красивой деревни.

Мы едем к староверам, это люди, которые живут очень закрытым сообществом, и практически никаких чужаков не просто не пускают, но даже не идут с ними на контакт. Они практически всегда отказываются от съемок, но мы постараемся все-таки с ними договориться. Мы едем в максимально труднодоступный поселок в Тыве, и попытаемся поговорить с ними.
Это Лядов, и как люди живут из староверских сёл.

snippet.title: COLLEGES ARE PANICKING STUDENTS AREN’T SHOWING UP!
snippet.description:
College enrollment is falling, universities are facing budget cuts and closures, and higher education leaders keep talking about the coming “enrollment cliff.”

But there’s another question:

What are students actually getting for the money?

In this video, we’re looking at falling college enrollment, rising tuition, student debt, college career outcomes, degree inflation, entry-level jobs, AI and whether a college degree still provides the same advantage it once did.

The United States has thousands of colleges and universities, but many schools are now preparing for a shrinking college-age population and declining enrollment.

Higher education leaders point heavily to demographics.

Americans had fewer children after the financial crisis, meaning fewer college-age students are now entering the system.

And that absolutely matters.

But students are also looking at the price of college, the job market waiting for them after graduation and whether the degree they’re buying actually produces the outcome they were promised.

When more people have degrees, having a degree alone does less to differentiate someone.

So people get master’s degrees.

Then PhDs.

Then employers say they’re overqualified.

Meanwhile, companies are adopting AI and changing the entry-level jobs that traditionally gave new graduates a place to start.

What’s strange is how little of the discussion around the enrollment crisis focuses directly on that.

How many graduates get jobs in the field they studied?

How much do those jobs pay?

How much debt did students take on to get there?

How long does it take for the degree to pay for itself?

Those seem like pretty important questions when colleges are asking students to spend four years and potentially enormous amounts of money on an education.

Universities are trying to differentiate themselves through new programs, student experiences, facilities and connections to future industries.

But teaching something employers need and actually getting graduates hired are not necessarily the same thing.

Ultimately, college has to provide value beyond simply checking a box on a job application.

So is college still worth it?

Or has higher education become too expensive for the outcomes many students are getting?

localized.title: COLLEGES ARE PANICKING STUDENTS AREN’T SHOWING UP!
localized.description:
College enrollment is falling, universities are facing budget cuts and closures, and higher education leaders keep talking about the coming “enrollment cliff.”

But there’s another question:

What are students actually getting for the money?

In this video, we’re looking at falling college enrollment, rising tuition, student debt, college career outcomes, degree inflation, entry-level jobs, AI and whether a college degree still provides the same advantage it once did.

The United States has thousands of colleges and universities, but many schools are now preparing for a shrinking college-age population and declining enrollment.

Higher education leaders point heavily to demographics.

Americans had fewer children after the financial crisis, meaning fewer college-age students are now entering the system.

And that absolutely matters.

But students are also looking at the price of college, the job market waiting for them after graduation and whether the degree they’re buying actually produces the outcome they were promised.

When more people have degrees, having a degree alone does less to differentiate someone.

So people get master’s degrees.

Then PhDs.

Then employers say they’re overqualified.

Meanwhile, companies are adopting AI and changing the entry-level jobs that traditionally gave new graduates a place to start.

What’s strange is how little of the discussion around the enrollment crisis focuses directly on that.

How many graduates get jobs in the field they studied?

How much do those jobs pay?

How much debt did students take on to get there?

How long does it take for the degree to pay for itself?

Those seem like pretty important questions when colleges are asking students to spend four years and potentially enormous amounts of money on an education.

Universities are trying to differentiate themselves through new programs, student experiences, facilities and connections to future industries.

But teaching something employers need and actually getting graduates hired are not necessarily the same thing.

Ultimately, college has to provide value beyond simply checking a box on a job application.

So is college still worth it?

Or has higher education become too expensive for the outcomes many students are getting?

Fernando, el hijo de Doña Carmen, llega apurado a su cocina sin saludar: le dijo a su mujer que el sábado estuvo con su mamá, y quiere que ella se lo sostenga.

Doña Carmen sigue envolviendo sus corundas para el churipo y le hace unas preguntas muy sencillas. Luego le cuenta algo que le pasó a su propia madre, y algo que sucedió el sábado por la noche que Fernando no sabía.
